items.title: Show HN: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin
items.author: iacguy
items.content:
Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer.

OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure).

We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]).

- One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM.

We noticed that past ~640 session-hours a month, one always-on 4 vCPU VM is cheaper than per-session E2B sandboxes, for example. So at scale, this setup would not only be faster than current SOTA coding agents, but also more cost-efficient.

Feel free to try via cloud for free [4] or self host. We would love any and all feedback, and happy to answer any questions! Full demo below [3].

A writing app that knows your whole book. As you write, it notices what connects and what's left hanging, and shows you where, in your own words. It never writes a word for you.

Your writing is never used to train AI. Mark a book private, and nothing of it goes to any AI at all.

items.title: Show HN: Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we use to build Mastra
items.author: codekarate
items.content:
Hi HN, we're Shane, Sam, and Abhi.

Almost two years ago, we shared Mastra, our open-source TypeScript agent framework, on Show HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43103073. It got a few hundred upvotes; a couple of weeks later our downloads had doubled, and we were off to the races.

Today we're sharing Mastra Factory, the open-source software factory we built to help maintain Mastra itself.

At Mastra, we now average nearly 4M downloads per week, and with Factory our team now merges hundreds of PRs a week across the mastra-ai GitHub org. Last week, Factory opened and merged 238 PRs, alongside 630 merged PRs from humans.

There's a lot of debate about what a software factory is. For us Factory is a configurable agentic kanban board that's @-taggable in Slack.

Under the hood, it uses Mastra’s durable agents for long-running sessions, our conversational memory system, a markdown based wiki with source citations to incorporate company knowledge, signals that subscribe to PR comments wired up into sessions, and a customizable cloud sandbox with our coding harness (working on supporting Claude Code, Codex etc).

When we started out, we modeled Factory around our existing workflow-oriented process (triage, plan, build, review, shipped). Three months later, we find ourselves mostly driving it through Slack vs a web UI.

We’ve seen more senior engineers kick off sessions in parallel (“triage the 20 oldest issues and let’s evaluate…”). We’re using bug and vuln scanners now, and we’ve closed our repo to outside contributors, asking folks to write detailed issue repros instead.

You can get started with `npm create factory`.

It’s fully open-source, so you can run it entirely on your infra (we also offer a hosted version). Comment here, we would love to know what you think!

items.title: Show HN: I made an audio-to-MIDI model 60x more efficient
items.author: hidude562
items.content:
we're introducing Dettato, a audio to transcription model that significantly beats MuScriptor - the next best open model - and scores a bit higher than mirelo's closed source model 'Mirelo v1.1 Pro' on their published benchmarks. all at just 20m parameters - roughly 65x smaller than muscriptor. Additionally, in training the model, we trained on absolutely no copyrighted recordings. the model isopen sourceand you can use its outputs for commercial purposes.

disclaimer with the benchmarks: it's difficult to gauge the true accuracy of the model for your use-case without trying it yourself. one thing my model performs poor on for instance, is splitting instruments correctly. In addition, this just spits out performance with a beat aligned. If you're looking for something that you can actually play(e.g sheet music), i'd reccommendsongscription orklangio - both are excellent tools by great companies that push the envelope of what's possible in this field forward.

the driving goal of kobimusic: to help musicians, not replace them. a part of that goal means following copyright law. we trained dettato on a mix of synthetic instrument recordings and solo instruments mixed in using the dataset. the rest of the instruments morph together ~20 soundfonts, using the 'soundfont babies'technique i published. no copyrighted recordings were used.

I began working on dettato about 10 months ago, but scrapped what I had in about April. The reason why was that I treated as a data problem - but in reality, the bottleneck is architecture. There are a lot of parellels that you can draw for (first model i made) and . both traditionally were tackled early on using algorithms. later, in both fields they plugged in giant components. These models would naturally become overfit to synthetic data, since globally the problems of and become different than if you treat it locally. But, for both you can reframe it as a local problem. For , using a detector model. For , a pitch-lane model.

overall, i hope both open and closed weight music retrieval companies can learn from this. The constraint of not using copyrighted recordings doesn't hold you back, but actually encourages innovation, and it's likely you'll end up with a better model in the end.

items.title: Show HN: Open-source, real-time object tracking for live video feeds
items.author: aryaman_darda
items.content:
I type "forklift" on a live warehouse camera, and tamserve finds and tracks both forklifts, including the one driving in. Then I add "person" without stopping it.

tamserve runs Meta's SAM 3 on live camera feeds. SAM 3's own tracker handles one recorded video at a time, runs at about 8 fps, and runs out of memory on long videos. tamserve uses SAM 3 to find objects every few frames and a lightweight tracker (EdgeTAM) to follow them in between, with one copy of each model shared across all your cameras.

* *Any object you name:* 4x faster than SAM 3's tracker, at 92% of its accuracy * *People:* 16 cameras at once, 14x less GPU per frame, and slightly more accurate than SAM 3 (89.6 vs 87.8 HOTA) * *Memory:* flat at 3.5 GB on a 3,000 frame video, where SAM 3 runs out at frame 423

*Worth a look if you're building:*

* Warehouse or factory safety (forklifts, pallets, hard hats) * Security or retail camera analytics * Home or elder care monitoring * Robotics, wildlife or lab monitoring * Annotation tools for long videos

`pip install "tamserve[sam3]"`

Please give me any and all feedback or edit tamserve to meet your needs, and a star helps if you find it useful!

items.title: Show HN: Unref – A Python dead code finder built on Ruff's parser
items.author: McAvey
items.content:
None of the newer alternatives to Vulture worked out of the box on my codebases, so I decided to build one.

The first version was in Python, then I switched to Rust for speed and to reuse Ruff's parser. It checks all of CPython in under a second.

It found lots of interesting dead code in my team's codebases, and it's the first time in years we've had a Python dead code finder in our CI.

Feedback is very welcome, especially dead code it misses.
